canberra.title: The Dog Stars is 2026’s most disappointing movie
canberra.snippet: Ridley Scott is one of the most successful and recognisable directors alive today. He is also one of the most diverse. He burst onto the ...
canberra.content:
The Dog Stars stars Australian Jacob Elordi and is the latest film by legendary director Ridley Scott. Photo: 20th Century Studios.

Ridley Scott is one of the most successful and recognisable directors alive today. He is also one of the most diverse.

He burst onto the scene with Alien in 1979, created cult classics like Blade Runner and was the man responsible for one of the best movies of all time, Gladiator.

While all of these movies, along with many others, including The Martian and American Gangster, are certified bangers, there are a handful of others that are equally as disappointing or flat-out awful.

His newest film, The Dog Stars, is frustratingly in the latter of those two categories.

The Dog Stars is a post-apocalyptic thriller that follows Jacob Elordi as Hig and his dog Jasper. Hig is a mechanic and pilot in a world that has been ravaged by a virus, leaving very few survivors, akin to the likes of I Am Legend.

During his flights, Hig often receives radio calls from other distressed survivors who are trying to survive this world. On a gathering mission, Hig lands near a farm occupied by a couple of the people who have made mayday calls, including Cima (Margaret Qualley) and Pops (Guy Pearce).

From here, the trio navigate the abandoned world and the typical ‘survive the apocalypse’ film takes place, albeit with a few twists and turns I won’t spoil here.

The key point I want to drive home about The Dog Stars is not that it’s bad. It’s that it’s frustratingly disappointing.

When Ridley Scott announces a new project, it really is a flip of a coin as to what kind of quality you’re going to get. Often, with Scott’s films, the quality of his script determines the quality of the film.

The issue here is that the script is painstakingly dull and, as a result, this movie is so … boring.

Say what you will about Scott’s work on Prometheus or Nepolean, but at least there was intrigue and innovation there. The Dog Stars takes its initially interesting premise and turns it into a narrative as bland as the setting it’s shot in.

It’s not the actors’ fault. Elordi is great, Qualley and Pearce try hard, and even Josh Brolin puts in a decent shift. The issues just come back to the script.

If there is nothing for the characters to do, there is nothing for the actors to go on. This, in turn, means the viewers have nothing to care about.

Let’s use Scott’s own work for reference.

Maximus from Gladiator is iconic. His story about leading the Roman armies before being betrayed by the Emperor’s son, who killed his family, is solid stuff.

From that alone, we know Maximus is a fighting leader; he has personal stakes in hating the antagonist and a reason to seek vengeance.

With Elordi’s Hig, we know nothing other than that he likes his dog. We get flashbacks, sure, but they don’t push the narrative the way Maximus’s story does. It’s more of a fill-in-the-blanks for an annoyingly mysterious character.

The film is shot fairly well, and the use of IMAX is very welcome, especially in some of the landscape shots, which are fantastic.

When the action does take place, particularly the sequences with the plane, it’s entertaining enough, but because the characters are so dull, there is no emotional difference between if they crash and die or miraculously make it out alive.

I really wanted to love The Dog Stars. The trailers gave me real hope, and the quality of 2026’s original films so far left me wanting more. I was hoping for some real Ridley Scott magic, but unfortunately, I called heads and the coin landed on tails.

The Dog Stars is showing in cinemas across the country.

canberra.title: New $124 million Gungahlin college to welcome students in 2029
canberra.snippet: In three years, 800 students will be able to walk through the doors of Gungahlin’s second college campus. The $124 million facility...
canberra.content:
Gungahlin’s second college campus is expected to open for the 2029 school year. Photo: Artist’s impression/Supplied.

In three years, 800 students will be able to walk through the doors of Gungahlin’s second college campus.

The $124 million facility is promised to be state-of-the-art, with a new performing arts theatre, gymnasium, tennis hard-courts and sports fields that will be available to the community outside of hours.

It will also be all-electric and powered by solar, with food technology classrooms, water-wise landscaping and active transport facilities.

Education Minister Rachel Stephen-Smith said it was about building the capacity of the public education system in Canberra’s north and easing pressure on the current Gungahlin College campus.

“We know that Gungahlin continues to be a growing community, and that the young families who’ve moved into some of the newer parts of Gungahlin have children who are getting older, and moving into college age,” she said.

“[This project will] enable young people in Gungahlin to study, play, and build their futures closer to home.”

Infrastructure Canberra’s Hayley Bell, Yerrabi MLA Suzanne Orr, Education Minister Rachel Stephen-Smith and Hindmarsh Construction project manager Elyse Francis all took part in the sod turn for Gungahlin’s second college campus. Photo: Claire Fenwicke.

Local construction firm Hindmarsh Construction won the tender to build the project.

Project manager Elyse Francis said early works approval was expected by the end of August.

“Education facilities are always a great project to be a part of, being able to see the incoming students really enjoy the best that our education facilities have to offer,” she said.

“Both of the buildings will [be built] concurrently. Building A being the majority of the teaching facilities, [and] Building B being the theatre and also the sports centre.

“We look to have most of our structure complete by mid next year, and then we’ll be focusing on our external works and building facades.”

The project is expected to support about 150 workers at the peak of construction.

The current Gungahlin College is part of a shared priority enrolment area with Dickson College.

This new facility won’t replace the current one, but will be another option for families in the north.

“The project is designed so that the school community can grow into the future,” Ms Stephen-Smith said.

“That will really be dependent on demand, but there’s certainly capacity built into the project to grow beyond the first year’s 800 students, as the need in the community grows and as people [potentially] move from one college to another.”

Gungahlin’s second college campus will cater for up to 800 Year 11 and 12 students in its first year. Photo: Artist’s impression/Supplied.

Priority enrolment areas across Canberra are under constant review by the Education Directorate, and at this stage it is not known if the catchment area will change once the college opens.

“It depends on what we’re seeing in terms of demand across all of the Northside colleges, and making sure that we really are balancing the enrollments across our schools so that they can all deliver excellent education and a variety of programs for year 11 and 12,” Ms Stephen-Smith said.

The second Gungahlin College doesn’t have its own name or uniform yet, but there’s plenty of time to sort out those details before opening.

It will be built in Nicholls near the Gold Creek School senior site.

It’s expected to open in time for Term 1, 2029.

For more information, visit Built for CBR.

canberra.title: Goodbye, Fiji flights. Hello, holiday hangover
canberra.snippet: Last week, I was in Fiji snorkelling through an underwater rainbow of tropical fish, following a flotilla of turtles cruising the current...
canberra.content:
From poolside views to post-holiday blues. It’s a journey. Photo: Hayley Nicholls.

Last week, I was in Fiji snorkelling through an underwater rainbow of tropical fish, following a flotilla of turtles cruising the currents, and watching world-class wipeouts at internationally revered surf spot Cloudbreak off Tavarua Island.

This week, Fiji Airways announced the suspension of direct flights from Canberra. Talk about a post-holiday buzzkill.

Officially, the blame lies with the usual culprits – global uncertainty and rising fuel prices – along with softer demand from travellers connecting to the United States.

I’m disappointed. We didn’t prove demanding enough for the express route to paradise.

To ease my misery, I’ve been reminding myself that returning home from Fiji isn’t a holiday. Regardless of the route taken, you may end up – like me – in holiday come-down hell.

I’m battling my way through roughly 1200 loads of washing and a similar backlog of emails. I’m swatting away Outlook reminders, school emails and texts from the post office threatening to return my uncollected packages. In the background, my neglected houseplants stage a dramatic protest, and the air-con unit begs me to clean its filters.

Oh, and it’s Book Week.

We have a fantastic life at home, for which I’m terribly grateful and all that. But please indulge me in a little foot-stomping as I struggle to adjust to “real life” after a resort-style getaway.

First, where is the buffet?

This is the most obvious bummer.

No longer can I start my day with dignity, rise at a leisurely pace and sleep-walk through aisles of freshly squeezed juices, towers of fresh fruit, and fried brekkie delights.

In Fijian paradise, the toughest choice each morning was: fried, scrambled or poached?

At home, an average school morning sees me wake with alarm (literal and figurative), before I’m launched headfirst into a gauntlet of lost lunchboxes, sibling spats and silly questions – and all before coffee. Which I have to make myself, by the way.

After breakfast is served, rather than sinking into a poolside daybed to quietly enjoy my food-coma, I’m scraping stale Weet-Bix off the kitchen counter. What a fall from grace.

Nothing is freshly cleaned daily.

With no magical little sign hanging from my door, there appears to be ZERO housekeeping service. Actually – it’s worse than that – I am the housekeeper.

What in the Freaky Friday is this cruel practical joke?

No crisp white sheets reappear daily. No freshly swept floors. Not a thoughtfully placed hibiscus flower in sight! Oh, it’s a cold dose of reality to find your dishevelled mess of a morning waiting to greet you again in the afternoon.

Fiji time > Outlook calendars

It took me ages to adjust to “Fiji time”. It was days before I exchanged my high-paced power walk for the slow shuffle of island life.

When I first spotted the resort’s activities board, every event felt like a make-or-break deadline (which obviously, a hermit crab race should not be). By the end of the week, I was forgetting to show up to things entirely – and could not care less.

It is very rude, therefore, to open my laptop and be assaulted by the colour-coded anxiety attack that is my Outlook calendar.

How did I end up with so many responsibilities that they need a system of categorisation?

Last week I was basically a drunk mermaid. How am I supposed to make this transition?

I just managed to slow myself down to the pace of a sea turtle, and sea turtles can’t be expected to do admin, appointments and other responsibilities.

In real life, I can’t just forget to show up to anything. First, there are too many text reminders; second, there are cancellation fees.

Neither of which was a problem last week when the biggest things on my to-do list were coconut bowling and karaoke.

Was the Bula! worth the backlog?

I may never recover from this holiday – financially, logistically, emotionally – and definitely not in terms of laundry. But I regret nothing!

My post-holiday come-down may have me feeling weathered, worn and whingey, but ultimately a step away from “real life” always offers fresh perspective.

We’re lighter on our feet as a family, trying to appreciate each other and avoid falling back into servitude to our phones. We’re stressing less about the little things, and I’m trying not to speedwalk everywhere as though I carry urgent word from the King.

Holidays remind us what’s important. It’s not the breakfast buffet or daily turndown service.

But sadly, this high-minded rhetoric does not help me with the washing.

canberra.title: Fifty years on, this Canberra classroom is still helping new arrivals find their voice
canberra.snippet: When Ahmed Al Haboush and Omar Gherablji arrived in Canberra from Lebanon in November 2023, they came on the same plane. Both were origin...
canberra.content:
Ahmed Al Haboush and Omar Gherablji outside the Edna Hopkins Library at Dickson College, named after the woman who established Canberra’s Introductory English Centre 50 years ago. Photo: Naziya Alvi.

When Ahmed Al Haboush and Omar Gherablji arrived in Canberra from Lebanon in November 2023, they came on the same plane.

Both were originally from Syria. Both families had fled the war and lived in Lebanon before being resettled in Australia. And both teenagers arrived with barely enough English to navigate their new lives.

They had gone to school in Lebanon, but English had played little part in their education. For Ahmed, even recognising the alphabet was a struggle.

Within days of arriving in Canberra, the boys found themselves in a classroom at the Secondary Introductory English Centre (SIEC) at Dickson College.

Today, they are in Year 12. They speak English, study alongside other Canberra students, play soccer, work and are preparing to graduate.

“Mr Cheater tried his best to help us and we learnt it,” Omer told Region.

Their story is one of thousands. This year marks 50 years since the late Edna Hopkins AM established Canberra’s Introductory English Centre to give newly arrived young people intensive English teaching before they entered mainstream schooling.

More than 6000 students have passed through the program since. And the classroom continues to change with the world outside it.

There are currently 43 students at SIEC, with two more enrolments pending at the time Region visited. The program can fluctuate dramatically according to migration and how quickly students progress: in the past four years it has had as few as 22 students and as many as 148.

Its young people come from across the world. SIEC executive teacher Reece Cheater said some of the largest groups have come from Syria, Saudi Arabia, China and Afghanistan. Just last week, the centre enrolled two Rohingya refugees from Myanmar who had fled to Bangladesh and grown up in camps in Thailand.

Refugees account for over half of the student population at SIEC. Many have had their schooling interrupted; some have had little formal education and others have never been to school at all.

That makes teaching English only one part of the job.

“For some of them, when they first arrive in Australia, they’re traumatised,” Mr Cheater said.

“They’ve faced displacement, lost family members, war. Some of them even have physical injuries from bomb blasts and things like that.”

Some young people take months before they are ready to talk about what they have experienced.

“Every person is an individual, and every person’s got an individual story,” he said.

Inside the classroom, that can mean teaching without initially relying much on spoken language at all.

Students at Canberra’s Secondary Introductory English Centre rehearse ahead of the program’s 50th anniversary celebrations. Photo: Naziya Alvi.

Teachers use pictures, gestures, written words, repetition and physical demonstrations. Early lessons are built around familiar themes such as “Me, Myself and I”, allowing students to learn English by talking about their families, cultures and their own lives.

And there is plenty of laughter. “One of the best things is humour,” Mr Cheater said.

The teachers, he jokes, are “a little bit of frustrated comedians”. But outside the classroom, not knowing English can make even ordinary encounters intimidating.

Ahmed recalled being unable to understand questions from people around him. A visit to the doctor with his father was particularly difficult as the pair struggled to follow what was being said. Even a simple bus ride was a nightmare when you don’t know the local language.

Omar remembers a tradesman coming to repair a broken window at home. The man talked. Omar and his brother couldn’t understand him.

“We just shook our heads,” he recalled.

Those encounters are funny to them now. At the time, they illustrated how isolating life can be when almost every interaction requires a language you don’t yet possess. SIEC has been changing that for students for 50 years now.

Students aged between 12 and 18 attend full-time, from 9 am to 3 pm, and can spend up to 12 months in the intensive program. But Mr Cheater said some of the most effective learning happens outside the classroom — playing soccer, finding work and making English-speaking friends.

“We’re giving them the literacy skills, the decoding skills to be able to make decisions about their lives and giving them opportunities that they wouldn’t have had,” he said.

For Ahmed and Omar, one year at SIEC was followed by Dickson College’s Refugee Bridging Program, which provides additional English and learning support while students participate in mainstream classes. They are now approaching the end of Year 12.

Teacher Cay Merritt’s connection to the program is even more personal.

When she and her husband adopted four children from Haiti in 2014, three attended an Introductory English Centre at Wanniassa Hills Primary School while their eldest daughter attended SIEC.

Ms Merritt spoke French and her children knew some French and Haitian Creole, but they still needed help making the transition into Australian education.

“I’m so grateful to the introductory English centres because that has really helped their English and helped them to go to school,” she said.

“The program for me was a lifesaver.”

Years later, Ms Merritt ended up teaching at the same program that had helped her own family.

Next week, former students, teachers and community members will come together to celebrate SIEC’s 50 years.

Fifty years ago, Edna Hopkins created a classroom where children arriving in a new country could find their words, their confidence and, eventually, their place in Canberra.

SIEC’s 50th anniversary celebration will be held at the Dickson College library from 4 pm to 7 pm on Thursday, 3 September. The event is open to all former and current students and staff, as well as members of the wider community.

canberra.title: Spotted a spotted quoll lately?
canberra.snippet: This column is prompted by a very special visitor to our campsite on a recent short holiday to some of the World Heritage rainforest park...
canberra.content:
Spotted-tailed Quolls are intelligent, bold and curious. This one wanted to know more about my insulated mug on the camp table. Photo: Ian Fraser.

This column is prompted by a very special visitor to our campsite on a recent short holiday to some of the World Heritage rainforest parks in north-eastern NSW. However this visitor has Canberra connections too, as it is the only quoll species now found in the ACT, hence this column.

The very handsome Spotted-tailed Quoll is the largest marsupial carnivore surviving on mainland Australia but is generally shy and keeps to more remote areas, in dense forest or rocky habitats.

They are robust, mostly rusty red with white spots, including on the tail as per the name. This distinguishes them from the other three Australian species, which are also considerably smaller. A big male Spotted-tailed Quoll can be nearly a metre long from nose to tail tip, and weigh at least five kilograms.

Until recently however the Spotted-tailed Quoll was only the third-biggest marsupial predator on the mainland, but the spread of dingoes over the past 4000 to 5000 years eliminated the thylacine and Tasmanian Devil from mainland Australia, both vanishing around 2500 years ago.

The one that visited our camp was, I think, a young male and he was very curious, unafraid and very agile, approaching us for a sniff and getting up onto the table and even the benchtop of our trailer without difficulty. I must say it was one of the highlights of my fairly long Australian natural history life.

Spotted-tailed Quolls are very proficient hunters; young quolls rely on small mammals, reptiles, birds and insects, while adults focus on medium-sized mammals such as possums, young kangaroos, small wallabies, bandicoots and rabbits as well as scavenging carrion. Most of their hunting is done on the ground but they also climb easily and well.

A 2005 study published in the prestigious Royal Society Proceedings compared the bite force of a range of modern carnivorous mammals, relative to their different body weights. Marsupials in general rated more highly than other mammals, and the Spotted-tailed Quoll’s bite ranked only just behind the Tasmanian Devil’s, and considerably above those of big cats, wolves, hyenas and bears.

Spotted-tailed Quoll inspecting the campsite in Werrikimbe National Park in northern NSW. But you could be as lucky in a Namadgi NP campground too! Photo: Ian Fraser.

They were very common locally in the 19th century but unfortunately they discovered the benefits of chook runs as a source of food and the reaction from our forebears was swift and brutal. In the early 1860s vast quantities of strychnine baits were laid and the abundant Spotted-tailed Quolls rapidly became very rare in the region.

The smaller Eastern Quoll was common then too, but since 1963 they have been extinct on the mainland, surviving only in Tasmania. Foxes, dogs and cats seem to have been the main culprits in their disappearance.

Surprisingly the last recorded Eastern Quoll population was in the Sydney suburb of Vaucluse. However there have been successful reintroductions – including at Goorooyaroo Nature Reserve in the northern ACT – into predator-proof sanctuaries.

Spotted-tailed Quolls however are still hanging on in the ACT and there have even been a couple of records from suburban Canberra in the past couple of decades. These include a road-killed quoll by Johnson Drive in Tuggeranong in 2016 and a very much alive one which sought refuge in a front yard eucalypt in Charnwood back in 2010. I recall that that one was reported initially as an ‘orange possum’, which I can easily understand, especially given that he was up in a tree.

He was eventually coaxed into a net by some bold and determined rangers and later released into Namadgi National Park. It seems that such wanderers are usually young males forced out of their fathers’ territories.

Spotted-tailed Quoll displaying the bite that ranks him number two in the world, taking size into account, among land-based carnivores. Photo: Ian Fraser.

Perhaps unexpectedly for what is such an unfamiliar animal group today, the word ‘quoll’ was one of the first Australian mammal names to be recorded in English. Joseph Banks learnt it from the local Guugu Yimithirr language speakers in the place where Cooktown now stands, when Cook’s crew was forced ashore for some weeks after damaging the Endeavour on a reef. He wrote it in his notebook as ‘je-quoll; he also recorded there the name ‘kanguru’ for the first time.

‘Quoll’ didn’t come into widespread use in Australia though until the 1960s. Until then they were just ‘native cats’ or ‘tiger cats’ for the big one, spots notwithstanding.

The area of north-eastern NSW where we encountered our very welcome guest is now Australia’s hot spot for them. It seems that extensive areas of natural forest with lots of tree and fallen log hollows, and abundant prey, plus a relatively low fox population, suit them well. How I’d love to see them commonly in the ACT again too.

australia.title: Pacific Islands Forum meeting in turmoil after several leaders pull out of Palau summit
australia.snippet: Solomon Islands prime minister cancels his appearance, along with leaders from Fiji, Vanuatu and Samoa Several leaders have pulled out of...
australia.content:
Several leaders have pulled out of a the Pacific Islands Forum leaders’ meeting in Palau at the eleventh hour.

Solomon Islands prime minister, Matthew Wale, has cancelled his appearance after a no-confidence motion was lodged against him at home by the Solomon Islands home affairs minister, Manasseh Maelanga.

Maelanga accused Wale of “repeatedly making decisions of matters of national importance without proper consultation with, or the approval of, cabinet, thereby undermining the principles of collective cabinet responsibility, representative democracy and good governance”, according to the ABC.

Australia has been in negotiations with the Solomons on a security treaty, with the hope that further negotiations could have taken place on the sidelines of the summit.

Fiji’s prime minister, Sitiveni Rabuka, and his Vanuatu counterpart, Jotham Napat, will also not be attending, with the Samoan leader, La’auli Leuatea Schmidt, another notable absence.

The Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has confirmed he will still be attending.

Oliver Nobetau, the Lowy Institute’s Pacific Islands program director, said the pulling out by key leaders “dulls the flame” of the meeting.

“This has been shaping up to be quite a significant PIF … it’s really unfortunate that this is the case,” he told Guardian Australia.

“With the pulling out of this many key prime ministers within the region, it dilutes the potential of what could come out of this leaders’ meeting.”

Nobetau said there were high expectations that this leaders’ meeting could progress pilot projects around Pacific climate resilience, and was important ahead of the Cop31 climate summit in November and a pre-Cop31 summit to be held in Fiji and Tuvalu in October.

He added the leaders not showing up could be read as those nations prioritising bilateral agreements with nations including Australia above region-wide commitments.

“PIF has to demonstrate its usefulness as well. While it is a useful forum for a lot of our Pacific members, maybe the bigger countries feel there are more pressing issues or they can achieve more benefits for their countries by engaging bilaterally or directly with other partners.”

Speaking at Queensland Labor conference on Sunday in Brisbane, Albanese said Australia had a duty to help Pacific nations thrive.

Albanese said allowing Pacific nations to succeed would also benefit Australia.

“The big challenges facing the Pacific require solutions designed and delivered for the Pacific, by the Pacific,” he told the

“Australia has a key role to play, as a partner and leader.

“In a time of strategic competition in our region, our engagement in the Pacific Islands Forum and our contributions to the infrastructure, regional security and climate action of the region matter more than ever before.”

The visit follows the prime minister signing a security deal with Fiji, elevating the bilateral relationship to a formal alliance as Australia seeks to curb Chinese influence in the region.

Pacific leaders are set to discuss security and climate concerns during the summit.

Albanese said Australia would also seek to reiterate support for Pacific workers coming to the country.

Debate has recently raged over how the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility Scheme cohort would factor into immigration cuts flagged by various parties.

Representatives of the resurgent One Nation have been pressed to clarify that PALM workers, many of whom provide much-needed labour in regional areas, would not be included in a significant reduction to net overseas migration.

Albanese said the migration discussion had been fuelling division and the Pacific worker scheme would continue because of its critical economic benefit.

“People from the Pacific make an enormous contribution to Australia’s prosperity through their vital work in regional industries like agriculture and meat processing,” he said.

“So many of our farmers and food producers rely on them.

“We know also the wages they remit home help boost the economies of their families and communities, contributing to the prosperity and stability of the whole region.”

australia.title: Renee was at Gyirong Port minutes before flood struck, now her family want to travel from Australia to help search
australia.snippet: Missing woman’s partner and daughters fundraise to join search in one of the hardest-hit areas of Nepal Follow our Australia news live bl...
australia.content:
Clair Spry says her sister would hate the attention. She would want it focused on the Nepali people, who have been displaced or are in need of aid. She would want it to be on the impact of the climate crisis, especially on the world’s most economically vulnerable populations.

“Her focus right now would not be on her; it would be on the families,” Spry said. “So many people, the Nepalese people, that have been horribly displaced and traumatised. She would want the attention on them and how we are going to help them.

“And global warming. This is something the poorest people of the world are affected by. It’s not the New Yorkers, it’s the people who are in these parts of the world. For Renee, that would be heartbreaking.”

Like many of the missing Australians, Renee arrived at Gyirong Port just 10 minutes before the flood struck. The area was one of the hardest hit – images from Chinese rescue teams show the area completely flattened. Huge buildings, power lines, everything – just wiped away.

Renee is a disability support worker who lives on the Sunshine Coast. She has been with her partner, Shaun, an emergency nurse, since they were 15, and they share two daughters in their 20s.

Clair has set up a GoFundMe to get the three of them over to Nepal – Shaun wants to travel to the port to try to find any signs of her. And their daughters, Lily and Ruby, don’t want him to go alone.

“Their first reaction is, we have to go. The practicalities, and what can actually be done in the first few days, it hasn’t been possible [to enter the area], but they still want to go,” she said.

“And if they are able to find her, to bring her home.”

Renee’s family understand how dire the situation is, and how unlikely it is that she, or anyone in that same area, survived. But until they know for certain, they would hold hope, she said.

“Everyone’s very realistic. We know how bad this was and where she was. But until they find her, everyone’s got this little slither of hope that maybe she’s stuck somewhere and can’t get out, or she’s injured.

“I’ve been looking through pictures trying to identify someone or see her. But we understand the reality of this situation.”

Like most Australians, Renee had come to Nepal on a pilgrimage. Spry said her sister was a “deeply spiritual” person who loved to help people.

“She had two degrees, and she chose to do something that was … a completely selfless vocation. Her priority was always other people,” she said.

“Every person she touched, they knew her love and kindness. She would be so uncomfortable with all this.”

The family of Michael Keats, an Australian who had been near the Tibet-Nepal border when flash flooding began, confirmed his death in posts to social media on Sunday.

Keats’s wife, Emily Boyd, said on Instagram he had been on a pilgrimage to Mt Kailash that had been a “dream for many years”.

“Mike went on a pilgrimage to Mt Kailash seeking enlightenment,” Boyd said.

“There’s a bittersweetness knowing that there was nothing more that Mike wanted then to know God, and to merge with the divine.

”He was a mystic, a medicine man, a teacher, leader, partner, father, brother, son, uncle and dearly beloved friend. He showed up for so many people in so many ways. A heart of pure gold. We love you forever and always.”

australia.title: ‘We owe it to history’ to defeat One Nation, PM tells Labor faithful – as it happened
australia.snippet: This blog is now closed Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Joyce explains One Nation’s migration policy with sh...
australia.content:
What we learned, Sunday 30 August

We’re going to wrap up our live news coverage today.

Here’s a recap of the day’s top headlines:

  • The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has told party faithful in Queensland that “we owe it to history” to defeat rightwing populism, amid a surge in support for One Nation and rising anti-immigration sentiment.

  • Pauline Hanson’s rightwing party won the Secret Harbour byelection in Western Australia on Saturday. Federal minister Tanya Plibersek said Labor would “have a good look” at the result but that the poll was largely held on state issues.

  • Plibersek also told ABC’s Insiders that the federal cabinet had never discussed cutting Australia’s refugee intake, contradicting reports this week.

  • The government is reviewing the import of smartglasses capable of recording video images, Plibersek says.

  • Missing Australian woman Cara Severino, who had lost contact with her family after flash flooding in Nepal, was safely located. Her family said they were “beyond relieved and elated”.

  • Speakers at anti-immigration rallies held across the country have taken credit for the surge in support for One Nation.

Key events

  • 7h ago

    What we learned, Sunday 30 August

  • 7h ago

    Mark Latham and right-wing activists address March for Australia rallies

  • 7h ago

    Man charged with murder of elderly woman in Tasmania

  • 7h ago

    March for Australia rallies claim credit for One Nation's rise

  • 8h ago

    Victorian Labor pledges to double pothole fixes if re-elected

  • 9h ago

    Family ‘beyond relieved and elated’ Cara Severino found safe

  • 9h ago

    We ‘owe it to history’ to defeat One Nation, PM tells Brisbane Labor conference

  • 10h ago

    Man dies after eighth-floor balcony fall in Sydney

  • 10h ago

    Joyce suggests One Nation would reject refugees from Nepal if country judged unsafe

  • 11h ago

    Man in police custody after suspicious death of woman in Tasmania

  • 12h ago

    Thirteen-year-old dies from head injuries after e-scooter crash

  • 12h ago

    Cabinet never discussed cutting refugee intake, says Plibersek

  • 12h ago

    Imports of smartglasses could face government regulation, says Plibersek

  • 13h ago

    Missing Australian woman Cara Severino found after Nepal floods

  • 13h ago

    Good morning

Mark Latham and right-wing activists address March for Australia rallies

Mark Latham and right-wing influencer Auspill were among the speakers at the “free speech” March for Australia rallies today.

Benjamin van der Linden, from a group called Make Australia Christian Again, posted footage showing Hugo Lennon, who goes by the name Auspill online, leading a march in Melbourne in chants of “Aussie, Aussie, Aussie”.

Latham, the former federal Labor opposition leader and ex-One Nation New South Wales state leader, was among the headline speakers at the Sydney rally today. He called for the abolition of “all the Chris Minns hate speech laws”.

The crowd booed when Anthony Albanese and Mehreen Faruqi’s names were mentioned, but the jeers were loudest when Minns, the NSW premier, was mentioned. Other Sydney speakers included Libertarian MP John Ruddick, Chris Yates from activist group CitizenGO and former federal Liberal MP Ross Cameron.

According to the March for Australia Facebook page, Brisbane’s rally was be addressed by Barclay McGain, a former young Liberal National party member and now in the conservative political action conference (CPAC); the far-right influencer Andre Mamet, known as Ausmaxx; and Harry Richardson, from the British Australian Community, an organisation for “celebrating the ongoing contributions to Australia by people of British Isles descent”.

Queensland police said about 400 people attended the Brisbane CBD rally where two men were directed to move on after “breaching the peace”, a spokesperson said. They said 50 people attended the city’s counterprotest.

NSW police said they issued three men move-on orders.

Man charged with murder of elderly woman in Tasmania

Tasmanian police say they have charged a 55-year-old Huonville man with the murder of an elderly woman in the early hours of Sunday morning.

They say the body of the woman, 85, was located at her Stride Street home at Huonville.

Detectives have now charged the 55-year-old man with murder and he will appear in court on Monday.

March for Australia rallies claim credit for One Nation's rise

Luca Ittimani

Hundreds of people have gathered in capital cities at rallies organised under the banner of anti-immigration March for Australia.

Over 300 people gathered for a “free speech” rally in Belmore Park in the Sydney CBD at midday. More than 70 police officers attended, including riot squad officers and mounted police on horseback. A counter-protest had been scheduled for Hyde Park.

Brian Marlow, founder of nationalist activist group Revive Australia, led the rally. Much of the crowd raised their hands when he asked if they had attended the first March For Australia in August 2025. Bec Freedom, who organised the first March For Australia in 2025, received a round of applause.

Marlow said the marches were responsible for One Nation’s subsequent rise in the polls, with the minor party now claiming close to 30% of primary votes and winning the Secret Harbour byelection in WA yesterday.

Marlow said of One Nation:

They’re romping it home in byelections. Unfortunately, they elected the wrong person in Farrer, David Farley, but we can handle that, we can deal with that later … We have shown that if we get together and we do not give an inch we can win.”

At least four attenders in Sydney wore One Nation shirts. March For Australia’s social media pages have been highly critical of the party in recent weeks for its confused endorsement of a net migration target of 130,000 people a year.

Attenders at Sydney’s rally cheered at the mention of “remigration” and an end to “mass” migration.

Victorian Labor pledges to double pothole fixes if re-elected

Victorian Labor has pledged to fix half a million potholes, AAP reports.

The premier, Ben Carroll, will fund the $352m election pledge to double the number of potholes fixed on Victorian roads by delaying planned removal of three level crossings.

“The condition of our roads is not good enough,” Carroll said on Sunday.

“I respect your money and I have made commonsense decisions to show how we can afford it.”

He said planners had identified $112m in savings by deferring the completion of level crossing removals in Highett and Mentone by one year, which will be added to the state budget’s $1.4bn allocation for roads.

The saving would allow Victoria to double the number of potholes fixed next year – from 250,000 to 500,000.

“This is part of my new direction: to spend our money wisely, to focus relentlessly on the basics, and that is what I’m here to do,” Carroll said.

He said most of the potholes will be removed when the weather is driest, in the second half of this year and into January.

Shadow minister for police, Brad Battin, questioned the timing of Carroll’s announcement, given an election is set for 28 November, and claimed Labor had “neglected” roads for 12 years.

“Five minutes before an election and all of a sudden Ben Carroll has found there’s potholes in Victoria,” Battin said.

“And now he’s come out with a small patch fix for a major problem in Victoria.”

In July, the Liberal-National opposition pledged to invest $5bn over four years to repair and rebuild Victoria’s roads, including the elimination of 1m potholes.

Their plan involves a 25% increase on current spending.

Police suspend search for pilot missing in remote NT

Northern Territory police say they’ve suspended search for pilot Bob Bramley, who is believed to have died in a plane crash in the Gulf of Carpentaria.

Bramley, 23, from Tasmania, was believed to be the only occupant of a charter plane that reportedly crashed off the coast of Groote Eylandt on Tuesday.

Police divers had found some pieces of aircraft debris.

In a statement, the NT police said that “following careful consideration of all available information” the search had been suspended, and Bramley’s family had been advised.

Police said the a multi-day search from the air and sea, including specialist divers, had already taken place.

“Every reasonable search option has been considered and undertaken. Our thoughts remain with the pilot’s family during what is an incredibly difficult time,” the police statement said.

“Northern Territory police will assess and action any new information should it become available.”

Family ‘beyond relieved and elated’ Cara Severino found safe

The family of Australian woman Cara Severino – who had been missing in flash flooding in Nepal – say news she is safe is a “miraculous gift” after days without news following the disaster.

Severino had been hiking in the region and was listed as missing after the disaster. She had limited phone reception and a flat battery, but was able to make contact with her family on Friday as she headed towards Kathmandu.

In a statement, her parents Debbie and Frank Severino said:

We are beyond relieved and so elated to have Cara safe and well and we can’t wait to hold her in our loving arms. This morning we are being enfolded in love by our church family who, along with so many of our family and friends, have been praying with us for this miracle. We thank Jesus for answering these prayers.

Seeing Cara’s name appear on my message bank, hearing her voice and now seeing her photo and speaking with her has been the most miraculous gift. We are incredibly thankful to the Australian Consular Response teams for locating her and bringing her to safety and for the care they are giving her and all the amazing work they are doing to locate others. We are so grateful to her Nepalese hiking partners who saw her through a harrowing several days of hiking in very difficult terrain, so thankful that they have all made it to safety.

The scale of this tragedy is staggering and amidst our personal joy we continue to stand in prayer with the many families here in Australia, in Nepal and around the world who have lost loved ones or are still waiting to hear from them, we know that the waiting is horrendous.

Albanese outlines battle plan against One Nation for working-class voters

Anthony Albanese’s speech to Queensland Labor delegates contains a roadmap for the party to take the fight to One Nation over traditional working-class issues.

His words were particularly relevant in a state that has arguably more of the sorts of areas – blue collar communities of outer-suburban and regional voters – where traditional Labor supporters are targets of Pauline Hanson’s insurgency.

It’s obvious – One Nation are not on the side of working people.

How is their plan to cut penalty rates going to help the people of Logan, or Gladstone, or Strathpine, or Ipswich, or Mt Isa?

The only mainstream political force in Australia that seeks to govern in the interests of the Australian people in their own right is the Australian Labor party.

The best way to defeat this coalition of chaos is to give Australians real hope of a better future. For their country. And for their families and themselves.

To stay positive. To be the party with the ideas that will make our people’s lives better, our economy stronger, our country safer, our environment cleaner.

We ‘owe it to history’ to defeat One Nation, PM tells Brisbane Labor conference

The prime minister’s speech to Labor delegates in Brisbane this morning contained a rallying cry for the party faithful amid the rise of One Nation, the morning after another political shock wave.

Anthony Albanese said it had become “a crucial time” for the Labor movement.

Across the world, hard-right populists are on the march.

Peddling politics that is dangerous, divisive, and downright dishonest.

We simply must defeat them. We owe it to history.

And we will defeat them.

They’ll say anything and do anything to win votes. Bend any facts. Peddle misinformation and disinformation. Turn Australian against Australian.

Albanese said: “Parties like One Nation have no serious answers to our problems” and reaffirmed the party’s support for multiculturalism.

Delegates, we unequivocally support multiculturalism because we know it’s part of Australia’s strength.

And because we believe every Australian is equal, whether they are Australian by birth or Australian by choice.

PM says Australia’s role in Pacific matters ‘more than ever’ ahead of regional summit

The prime minister says Australia will remain “a partner and a leader” in the Pacific, as he prepares to take part in regional talks this week, AAP reports.

Anthony Albanese will attend the Pacific Islands Forum in Palau from Monday.

On Sunday, addressing the Labor faithful at the party’s Queensland state conference, he said allowing Pacific nations to succeed would also benefit Australia.

The big challenges facing the Pacific require solutions designed and delivered for the Pacific, by the Pacific.

In a time of strategic competition in our region, our engagement in the Pacific Islands Forum and our contributions to the infrastructure, regional security and climate action of the region matter more than ever before.

Albanese also reaffirmed his support for workforce schemes that bring Pacific Island labour to Australia, amid domestic debate about immigration.

“People from the Pacific make an enormous contribution to Australia’s prosperity through their vital work in regional industries like agriculture and meat processing,” he said.

“So many of our farmers and food producers rely on them.

“We know also the wages they remit home help boost the economies of their families and communities, contributing to the prosperity and stability of the whole region.”

Man dies after eighth-floor balcony fall in Sydney

A man died after he fell from a balcony on Sunday morning in Sydney, prompting a critical incident review.

New South Wales police said they attended an apartment block in Elizabeth Bay, east of Sydney’s CBD, before 8am today as part of ongoing investigations.

Kings Cross police attended an eighth-floor apartment to speak with a 40-year-old man, but a 38-year-old woman spoke to the officers and refused to let them in the unit. The woman left soon after, police said.

Officers stayed outside the unit but then heard that a man had fallen from a balcony. They then found the 40-year-old man and provided assistance until paramedics arrived and treated him for critical injuries. The man died at the scene.

Police said they established a crime scene and a critical incident team from another police area command would investigate the circumstances. The Professional Standards Command will review that investigation, with oversight from the Law Enforcement Conduct Commission, police said.

Police said it was unclear whether the man fell or jumped, but his injuries were consistent with falling from eight floors. They declined to say what the investigation was into, but said police would contact the woman.

Joyce suggests One Nation would reject refugees from Nepal if country judged unsafe

Barnaby Joyce says a One Nation government would avoid taking refugees from flood-ravaged Nepal if the department advised Australians to avoid travelling there.

The MP refused to say outright whether One Nation planned to cut Australia’s refugee intake or permanent migration in an interview on News24. But he raised Nepal, unprompted, as an example of the party’s principle for blocking immigration.

Asked if he agreed the refugee program should be cut, Joyce said:

The refugee program has got to work within a policy structure we’ve got. Remember, we’ve clearly stated that if an area, the Department of Foreign Affairs says it’s too unsafe to go there, then it’s unsafe to bring people from there and away from there, like such as places in Nepal. I presume that the Department of Foreign Affairs says it’s not unsafe to go to Nepal, but I wouldn’t be going there at the moment ...

The government at present only advises Australians to reconsider their need to travel to certain areas within 50 kilometres of central Nepal’s Trishuli River, and to exercise caution otherwise.

Asked if One Nation would hypothetically stop bringing Nepali people here were the department to advise against travelling there, Joyce said:

Well, I don’t know what Dfat’s position is right now and whether it covers the whole of Nepal. I know the Nepalese community have a huge say in sections of our country and the workforce, but they do it [arrive in Australia] within the visa category. And if they do come in, they’ll be within the Nom [net overseas migration].

Asked “are you happy with the refugee program at 20,000, yes or no,” Joyce said:

It fits within the Nom. That is our policy. And the refugee policy, it’s not that it’s dispensed, but you can’t come from countries which are dangerous. Like if you can’t go there, you shouldn’t be coming here.

Earlier, Joyce declined to say what outcome a One Nation government would seek for permanent migration, a different measure. He declined to say even whether it would be below Labor’s target of 180,000.

I would suggest, Andrew, very, very strongly that it would be, but I’m not going to go into the sort of the, you know, the, the, the peculiarities of what two numbers make up net.

You can read more about this week’s debate on migration numbers here:

Man in police custody after suspicious death of woman in Tasmania

A man is in custody as police investigate the suspicious death of a woman early this morning in Tasmania’s southeast.

Tasmania police said a woman was found deceased inside her home in Huonville on Sunday morning and officers were called to the scene at about 4.30am.

On arrival, officers determined the death was suspicious, police said. Criminal investigators, forensics and other specialist officers were at the home this morning to examine the circumstances of the woman’s death.

Police said they had taken a man into custody to assist investigations.

australia.title: One Nation’s Secret Harbour byelection win shows Labor is at a loss when it comes to calming angry voters | Analysis
australia.snippet: Even after a week in which Pauline Hanson and One Nation candidates tripped over themselves trying to explain key policies, voters still ...
australia.content:
The One Nation hype machine went into overdrive after Saturday’s Secret Harbour byelection but one thing is clear from the thumping victory.

Despite the party’s sustained surge in public support, Labor and the Coalition still don’t have any idea how to calm an angry electorate and dint support for Pauline Hanson and her insurgent movement.

Even before One Nation’s Luke Herdegen was confirmed as having easily defeated Labor’s Georgia Tree in the suburban Western Australia seat previously held by Labor, One Nation’s WA leader, Rod Caddies, declared there were “no safe Labor seats in this state or in this country any more”.

By Sunday morning, Nationals defector Barnaby Joyce said “politics has changed” in favour of One Nation, even claiming the polls were underplaying One Nation’s support nationally.

The party was on track for a swing towards it of more than 20% against Labor in the beachside electorate, a result Hanson said revealed deep-seated and growing anger towards the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, and the federal Labor government.

Although it is easy to overstate the significance of single byelection results, when voter behaviour is often quite different from general elections, the win shows under the right conditions, Hanson has the capacity to take seats from Labor, as well as the Liberals and Nationals.

Unless there is a significant shift between now and the next federal election, due in early 2028, incumbent MPs from all sides should fear One Nation and a voting electorate that appears increasingly ready to burn the whole show down.

It has mattered little that Hanson and her motley crew in Canberra had a terrible week, tripping over themselves seemingly every day trying to explain One Nation’s immigration policy, the key issue for the party’s base.

Since the Farrer One Nation MP, David Farley, failed to explain where cuts to lower net overseas migration would come from on TV last Sunday, Hanson and Joyce have both repeatedly flubbed their explanation of what Farley had actually meant to say. One Nation’s strategist James Ashby even appeared on News 24 after dark with a mop, admitting a clean up job was required.

Taking in part of Perth’s southern coastal suburbs, Secret Harbour sits almost entirely within the federal electorate of Canning, held by Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie.

Hanson, her billionaire benefactor, Gina Rinehart, and many One Nation supporters hold a special dislike for Hastie, because he gave evidence against accused war criminal and Victoria Cross recipient Ben Roberts-Smith. But Hastie was right in criticising the Liberal campaign under state leader and former television host Basil Zempilas.

Lackluster opposition to One Nation, in the misguided belief that any loss for Labor was a win for the Liberals, has left Zempilas and his diminished party wanting on Sunday. The best defence he could offer before the loss was to complain that the Liberals would have fared better in a byelection held in a seat closer to the Perth CBD.

Hastie’s message is right. Only a strong, values-led fightback against Hanson, including linking her to the US president, Donald Trump, is the way to fight back. Wishy-washy answers about preference deals and hypothetical minority government arrangements are misguided. The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, should take note.

On Sunday, Albanese told the Labor faithful in Queensland that the party owed it to history to defeat Hanson’s dangerous, divisive, dishonest politics. Fighting back on hip pocket issues still remains Labor’s best chance of stopping Hanson from winning enough seats to really change things in Canberra.

The next federal election is more than a year away, but the Secret Harbour result is the latest evidence of the failure of the major parties to effectively put One Nation back in its box.

australia.title: Australia could make social media algorithms optional and follow UK ban on pornography depicting strangulation
australia.snippet: Social services minister says social media was playing a role in the increase of sexual violence among teenagers Follow our Australia new...
australia.content:
The Australian government is considering allowing users to opt in or opt out of social media algorithms, and is looking at a recent UK ban on depictions of strangulation and suffocation in pornography.

The social services minister, Tanya Plibersek, said social media was “playing a huge role” in the increase in sexual violence among teenagers and choking, and confirmed the options were being considered as the government develops its second action plan to end family and domestic violence against women and children.

It follows the death of a 16-year-old girl in Sydney after a suspected sexual strangulation act. Guardian Australia reported on Thursday that a source informed about the case said the teenager was believed to have become unconscious as a result of asphyxiation during sexual intercourse, often referred to as “choking”. No arrests have been made.

Plibersek told the ABC’s Insiders program on Sunday that social media algorithms are deliberately feeding boys and men violent content and normalising strangulation during sex.

“If you set up a social media account as a young boy in Australia today, it takes an average of 23 minutes for you to be fed misogynistic, violent misogynistic content online. That is a deliberate decision of the social media companies that is wrecking our young boys, giving them all of the wrong ideas about what healthy relationships look like,” Plibersek said.

“It is no coincidence that 60% of young people now report that they’ve experienced strangulation during a sexual encounter … It is pervasive and widespread and deadly, and it’s being fed to our young people and normalised.”

Chanel Contos’s Teach Us Consent has campaigned for algorithms to be opt-in only on social media.

Plibersek said the government was working with the group and considering how to potentially design an opt-in or opt-out system for algorithms.

“We’re absolutely up for work on algorithms. Opting in to those recommender algorithms that are causing so much harm, opting in or opting out,” she said.

“We’re also, of course, looking very closely at the recent Meta case in the US [and] the moves that the UK government have introduced to prevent the depiction of strangulation and suffocation in pornography. These are all really important considerations as we develop our next action plan on family domestic and sexual violence, so that work’s going on right now.”

The government legislated a ban on social media for under-16s which took effect in December, and has also introduced age-verification for pornography. But Plibersek has previously conceded children were easily able to dodge the new rules.

Labor will also soon begin consultation on a digital duty of care bill that will put the onus on tech companies, including AI companies, to make online spaces safer for all users.

Plibersek said the digital duty of care legislation, as well as a second round of privacy reforms, could also help tackle camera-equipped smartglasses, which she said she had serious concerns about.

“Tech companies should know that their products are safe and make them safe before they release them on to an unsuspecting public. I know the Attorney-General has asked the privacy commissioner to look specifically at these glasses,” Plibersek said.

“We’ve got a second tranche of privacy legislation coming up soon as well … things like this that can be used to furtively film, including during sexual encounters, for that filming then to be made public or used against someone who is being filmed as a way of blackmailing them, I am very concerned about the potential uses of these glasses.”

world.title: Humanitarian crisis worsening in refuge for civilians fleeing Sudan’s civil war
world.snippet: Conditions are deteriorating in city of El Obeid and camps on its outskirts, with more people arriving every day Humanitarian conditions ...
world.content:
Humanitarian conditions in the Sudanese city of El Obeid and two camps on its outskirts are dire and deteriorating, according to people on the ground, as civilians displaced by fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces and Rapid Support Forces (RSF) militia continue to pour in from the surrounding countryside.

The UN says more than 15,000 families have arrived since mid-July, joining more than 200,000 people who arrived in the first half of the year, according to government figures cited by Save the Children.

“The situation is very harsh and is deteriorating as El Obeid is receiving IDPs [internally displaced people] on a daily basis … The city is shockingly overcrowded,” said Maryam, a humanitarian volunteer whose name has been changed for her safety.

The new arrivals came on foot, carrying almost nothing, she said. “They also suffer from a shortage of food and they definitely arrive traumatised.”

The city, the capital of North Kordofan province, was home to around half a million people before the war broke out more than three years ago.

While many of the new arrivals have been absorbed into the city, tens of thousands are living in two main tented camps. According to analysis of satellite data by the Yale Humanitarian Research Lab, 800 new tents appeared in one of the camps between 4 and 25 August.

“During my visit, I saw 450 arrivals coming from the surrounding villages just that morning,” said Paul Byars, the Sudan country director for the Danish Refugee Council, who was in El Obeid last week. “The authorities’ estimates are correct, that 85% of them are women and children. Most of the men are staying behind because this is the only time for farming.”

Civil war erupted in Sudan’s capital, Khartoum, about 250 miles (400km) north-east of El Obeid, on 15 April 2023, when a power struggle between the armed forces and RSF descended into open conflict.

Since then, about 11.3 million people have been displaced, more than a fifth of the population. Some parts of the country, including El Obeid and surrounding areas, are at risk of famine.

Estimates of the number of people killed in the war range from tens to hundreds of thousands. More than 10,000 people are thought to have been massacred by the RSF in El Fasher over two days when they seized the city in Sudan’s western Darfur region in October 2025 after an 18-month siege.

A surge in RSF drone strikes on El Obeid and nearby areas in June led the UN to warn that the city could face a repeat of what happened in El Fasher.

The number of strikes has since fallen. The armed forces also recaptured a key road leading north to Khartoum in late July, which at least partly lifted the threat of besiegement. However, drones are still killing and injuring civilians, while violence rages in the surrounding districts, pushing people to the city.

Recently, volunteers in El Obeid had noticed more “double-tap” drone strikes, where a second drone follows the first, hitting rescuers at the scene, Maryam said. “It is hard, so hard, living with this, hearing the sound of a drone hitting somewhere,” she said. “It’s very disturbing.”

Sudan’s civil war has become dominated by drones, accounting for half of all violent incidents, up from 4% at the start of the war, said Nohad Eltayeb, who monitors Sudan for Acled, a conflict tracking group.

Both sides used drones, but the RSF’s usage had become more volatile since the US war with Iran began to interrupt supply lines in February, she said. “They rely on fewer, very targeted strikes.”

So far this year, there have been 322 incidents of violence affecting civilians in the wider Kordofan region, compared with 388 for the whole of 2025, according to Acled data. While the RSF was responsible for half of those, the SAF has also killed and injured civilians. On 10 August, armed forces and an allied militia killed five civilians and injured 10 about 60 miles north-east of El Obeid, according to Emergency Lawyers, a non-governmental group.

With the threats to delivery trucks, food prices have rocketed. In north Kordofan in July, according to World Food Programme data, a litre of groundnut oil cost 17,000 Sudanese pounds (£21), up from 13,000 in June and 7,700 a year ago. The prices of wheat flour and goat and sheep meat have also more than doubled in the last year.

Meanwhile, El Obeid’s power and water infrastructure still has not fully recovered from RSF drone strikes in June.

“The main problem is the big [water] source that is in the north of the city has been severely damaged and it has not been repaired,” said Esperanza Santos, an emergency coordinator in Sudan for Médecins Sans Frontières. “The water pipes in the city have [also] been impacted. So mostly, both in the city – for example, in the hospital – and also in the IDP camps, they are relying on water trucking and it’s not enough.”

Conditions in the camps were poor too, Santos said. “In terms of sanitation, it’s very, very bad. It’s not enough. The ratio of latrines per person is impossible – there are more than 100 people for a latrine. So basically there is open defecation.”

Maryam said she and her fellow local volunteers remained committed, despite the difficulties. “The situation is deteriorating, but we are trying to stay together, to stay strong in the face of the drone attacks and the influx of IDPs … We are living with this and we hope things will become better.”

world.title: Egyptian queen’s 673-diamond necklace stolen in Vienna smash-and-grab raid
world.snippet: Police hunt two suspects after historic 200-carat piece is snatched from Austrian museum during opening hours Austrian police are hunting...
world.content:
Austrian police are hunting two men alleged to have stolen a 200-carat platinum necklace encrusted with 673 diamonds that was on loan to a museum in Vienna and once belonged to Egyptian royalty.

Authorities in the capital released pictures of the suspects captured by security cameras during the heist at the Museum of Applied Arts (MAK), amid a rash of spectacular smash-and-grab thefts from European cultural institutions.

The unmasked men bought tickets to the exhibition before shattering a glass display case with a hammer during opening hours on Thursday afternoon and making off with the diamond necklace.

In an appeal for information from the public, police said: “The perpetrators fled with the jewellery in an unknown direction.”

Officers fanned out through the city centre and deployed a police tracking dog to search for the suspects. The Kronen newspaper said investigators believed the men were probably carrying out a “contract job” on behalf of a criminal gang.

MAK said the piece had been snatched from a jewellery exhibition that had been on display since June, featuring more than 300 works by the French designers Van Cleef & Arpels. No one was hurt, although there were several witnesses in the room at the time.

Documentation for the show said the necklace once belonged to Queen Consort Nazli of Egypt, who wore it at the 1939 wedding of her daughter Fawzia to Iran’s then crown prince, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, who later became shah. The necklace was sold by Sotheby’s in New York in 2015 for $4.3m.

The MAK said the exhibition brought together about 200 “unique and rarely seen objects” from its own collection and pieces spanning the 120-year history of the Parisian jewellery house, from the Van Cleef & Arpels patrimonial collection.

A guided tour planned for Friday afternoon was listed as “cancelled” on the museum website and the exhibition, which was due to end on 27 September, was temporarily closed.

European museums have been hit by a string of high-profile heists since thieves broke into the Louvre museum in Paris during the day last October and escaped within minutes with crown jewels worth €88m.

In Spain on Thursday, thieves raided the Treasure of Villena, a collection of bronze age gold artefacts described as one of Europe’s most important prehistoric hoards.

This month, four of the most important works by the 15th-century Renaissance master Antonello da Messina were stolen during a national holiday from a museum in the Sicilian port city of Messina.

Two days earlier, Italian police said they had recovered three paintings by the French masters Paul Cézanne, Pierre-Auguste Renoir and Henri Matisse that were taken this year from a private museum near the northern city of Parma.

A report by Europol this month found that robberies at European museums are becoming increasingly violent, with thieves sometimes brandishing guns, assaulting staff and using sledgehammers, axes and even explosives to smash their way to targeted loot.

world.title: What could Meta’s US settlement mean around the world – and what now for other claims against firm?
world.snippet: Other governments could seek similar concessions, while separate legal action is pending in places ranging from Kenya to the Netherlands ...
world.content:
In October 2021, Abrham Meareg’s father, a professor of chemistry in Ethiopia’s northern town of Bahir Dar, was shot at close range and died outside his family home. This was in the middle of the country’s civil war.

For weeks, Facebook’s algorithm had actively promoted posts calling for the academic to be murdered, according to Meareg and Foxglove, a nonprofit organisation supporting Meareg’s lawsuit against the company in Kenya. These posts included photos of his father and his home address.

Meareg filed the lawsuit in 2022. He said he repeatedly asked Facebook to remove the posts and the company did nothing. Nearly four years later, the case has still not been heard. Foxglove said Meta, Facebook’s parent company, had “fought tooth and nail to avoid responsibility”.

Meareg said: “It’s a matter of numbers to them, a matter of statistics. It has been proven multiple times that our lives do not matter to them.”

On Wednesday, Meta settled a lawsuit brought by 29 US states who argued it had designed addictive products that hooked young people. The social media company agreed to pay $18bn and to change certain features of its platform in the US. California’s attorney general said it was a victory that would make “a world of difference for children and their families”.

But elsewhere in the world, in jurisdictions as far flung as Amsterdam and Nairobi, other claims have yet to be heard. Far bigger questions about the power of a single US technology company to shape politics and democracy everywhere on Earth are still to be answered.

For the US, the settlement is a victory. A jury has done what the US Congress could not – put controls on a powerful tech company. As a part of the settlement, Meta has said it will set time limits on children’s use of its platforms Facebook and Instagram and block night-time usage.

For Meta, the settlement is also a victory. Its share price rose in the hours after the deal was announced. Its CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, was not forced to testify. The sum it is to pay, while not meaningless, is far less than the states had sought – $200bn – or the amount Meta itself had suggested in a court filing it might have to pay, which was up to $1.4tn.

For the rest of the world, however, the picture is more mixed. The limits Meta will put on its US platform are, in large part, similar to limits the UK and Australia have already achieved through regulation. There are certain concessions Meta has now made that other governments could also demand: for example, while the UK plans to ban under-16s from social media platforms, it may wish to ask Meta to impose a default daily use limit of two hours for under-18s, which is what the company has agreed to in the US.

None of this meaningfully changes the equation for Meareg or what his case represents, which is that a massive US company, unaccountable to voters, unbound by transparency requirements, owns a worldwide digital commons that shapes reality for billions of people.

Whether courts and governments outside the US have the power to confront this fact is a far thornier question.

The central issue of Meareg’s case is Meta’s algorithm. This is the system that decides what content to show users of Facebook and Instagram. It sees you linger over a video about knitting sweaters, for example, and then decides you’ll like one about how to care for your spider plant.

It sees teenage girls watch diet content and shows them anorexia influencers. It sees young men search for bodybuilding content and shows them Andrew Tate. It is alleged to have amplified content that promoted the ethnic cleansing of the Rohingya in Myanmar. It contributed to the election victory of Donald Trump.

Meareg’s lawsuit rests on the claim that this algorithm promoted the posts that called for the death of his father, and that Facebook’s sparse moderation in east Africa did almost nothing to prevent this.

In the early days of the Meta trial in the US, it seemed plausible that states would push the social media firm to finally make some changes to this algorithm. Those changes had the potential to fundamentally alter how the company does business. Meta’s algorithm is intended to keep users scrolling, stuck on the platform, and then it shows them ads.

But that is not what appears to have happened. The terms of the settlement will slightly change what is shown to minors, in that they will not necessarily have personalised feeds. But it is hard to see this concession changing the equation in war zones or creaking democracies.

Arturo Béjar, an ex-Facebook employee and whistleblower, said the limitations were “the equivalent of saying: ‘Well, you can smoke as many cigarettes as you can in two hours a day.’ It doesn’t make the cigarettes any safer.”

It may be up to groups and individuals elsewhere in the world to try to push for these larger changes. It will be an uphill struggle.

In Kenya, the high court recently ruled that Meareg’s case against Meta could go ahead, after years of legal manoeuvring from the company to try to prevent it. It could now be heard in the next year.

Rosa Curling, Foxglove’s co-executive director, said: “Meta’s lawyers have spent years trying to prevent this important case being heard, thankfully without success. We hope that the news from the US is a sign that Mark Zuckerberg’s time is finally up.”

In the Netherlands, Repro Uncensored, a nonprofit organisation tracking digital censorship, hailed the US settlement as a “major victory”. Repro Uncensored has an ongoing legal case against Meta in the Netherlands for alleged discrimination against queer accounts, and plans further action in other European countries.

Martha Dimitratou, Repro Uncensored’s executive director, said: “The next stage of accountability must address not only addictive design but algorithms, discriminatory moderation and automated decision-making. These systems shape civic participation and democracy, and the companies controlling them must be held accountable globally.”

The European Commission released a charge sheet against Meta this summer saying the company’s features, including its infinite scroll, contributed to “unhealthy habits and compulsive use”.

That charge sheet is part of an investigation into Meta that the commission launched in 2024. It may lead to Europe pushing for larger changes from Meta, including to its personal algorithm.

It is unclear whether any of these groups or parties can succeed. Meta appears to fear US regulators and courts: after all, it caved after just four days of its US trial. It does not appear to be as intimidated by regulators elsewhere.

Earlier this year it managed to dodge a class-action lawsuit brought by a group of Rohingya refugees over its alleged role in contributing to a genocide in Myanmar. It will have the help of the Trump administration in opposing any EU regulation that could curb its reach in Europe.

Meta declined to respond to questions about either Meareg’s or Repro Uncensored’s cases. In an earlier response to whistleblower allegations that it fuelled violence in Ethiopia and Myanmar, it pushed back forcefully, saying it was “just not true” that the company put profits over safety. Regarding Meareg’s case, it has said it employs staff with local knowledge and expertise to “catch violating content” in Ethiopia.

Meareg said he believed that Meta expected him to give up. “They don’t know how I am determined for justice,” he said. “It is the thing you do for the person you love. If you love someone – and I loved my dad from my heart – then he needs justice. He needs a public apology. There has to be accountability.”

world.title: UK urged to help free British-Egyptian ‘arrested in Cairo over sister’s activism’
world.snippet: Lawyers claim Eman el-Shazly, from Birmingham, was detained in effort to silence her sister, a critic of Sisi regime The UK Foreign Offic...
world.content:
The UK Foreign Office has been asked to intervene to secure the release of a British-Egyptian woman who it is claimed has been arrested in Cairo because of her sister’s political activism.

Eman el-Shazly, a 45-year-old based in Birmingham, was arrested on 16 August while visiting Egypt. Her lawyers say she has been detained in an attempt to silence her sister Mona, a relentless and harsh critic of the Egyptian government on her UK-based YouTube channel.

Her two brothers have already spent three years in jail and, in May, were rearrested. They were previously held in pre-trial detention, facing charges of “promoting the ideas of a terrorist organisation on social media, as well as broadcasting false news harmful to state security”.

The UK Foreign Office has confirmed to the husband of Eman that she is being held in the Ramadan rehabilitation centre and her case has been given the same file number as that of her two brothers, Hassan and Eid.

The government of President Abdel Fatah al-Sisi has faced allegations that it frequently arrests relatives of political critics to put indirect pressure on the dissidents to end their overseas criticism of his rule or of state corruption. Much of Mona’s activism focuses on alleged cases of corruption inside the security services or public utilities, a highly sensitive subject in Egypt.

Arfan Rashid, the lawyer acting for Eman’s husband with whom she has four children, says that unlike Mona his wife has never been involved in politics, and had gone to Cairo two months ago to look after her ill mother after the arrest of her two brothers.

“There is ample evidence that Eman has been arrested to silence Mona,” Rashid said. He added that Eman had told the security officials she was no longer in contact with her sister, and that many family members had repeatedly asked her to stop her political activism in the UK, but to no effect.

Mona confirmed to the Guardian that she had been asked to halt her activism by other family members, including to take down her YouTube videos.

But she added: “I have done nothing wrong nor broken any law … I am a very strong woman, but it is very traumatic for me since 11 or 12 children are without their parents. It is a horrible situation, but the Egyptian government will not stop if I appear weak. The government is close to collapsing.”

Rashid said the UK government had recognised the practice of “punishment by proxy” in Egypt in its country profile policy and information note published in March 2026. Human Rights Watch and the House of Commons library warned in 2021 of an escalating pattern in which Egyptian family members of critics living abroad were being targeted.

Mona runs a YouTube channel in the UK that has 130,000 subscribers. She is also active on X, making specific and controversial claims about government officials.

The UK’s Foreign Office representation in Cairo has asked for access to see Eman but has not yet received a positive reply.

Eman’s husband, Zeesharn Moustapha, has said Egyptian police and security officers attended the family home where she was staying a few days before the arrest, and demanded that Eman tell Mona to stop publishing material against the Egyptian government.

On X, Mona has claimed as many as five members of her family have been detained or harassed by the Egyptian authorities. She wrote: “Kinship is something beyond my family’s will, and I invite them to disown me to save themselves from this despicable, illegitimate dictator. I am the one opposing Sisi, not five individuals from my family. This is a crime against humanity that does not lapse with time.” She has lived in the UK for 18 years.

Eman became a British citizen through marriage. Her lawyer has asked whether Alistair Burt, the UK’s new envoy on complex consular cases, should be asked to intervene by the Foreign Office. Burt was appointed a month ago and has been tasked with working to secure the release of British citizens held abroad.

Burt has already met Gurpreet Singh Johal, the brother of Jagtar Singh Johal, who has been detained by the Indian authorities for nearly nine years without a conviction.

The Foreign Office has been approached for comment.

world.title: South African police arrest two Thai men for allegedly smuggling parrot eggs
world.snippet: Bird eggs intercepted in homemade incubators at Johannesburg airport as officials try to halt wildlife trafficking South African police h...
world.content:
South African police have arrested two Thai nationals in separate incidents for allegedly attempting to smuggle endangered parrot eggs out of the country as authorities try to stem the tide of wildlife trafficking.

A 50-year-old Thai national was arrested at OR Tambo international airport in Johannesburg on 20 August, carrying 50 bird eggs in a homemade incubator in a hand-luggage bag, South Africa’s environment ministry said in a statement.

The ministry said preliminary investigations indicated that the eggs were from parrot species listed under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (Cites), which regulates international trade in wild animals and plants to ensure species do not become extinct. It did not specify which species.

Another Thai national, a 23-year-old, was arrested at the same airport on 16 July, allegedly trying to smuggle 418 parrot eggs in two homemade incubator bags. Thailand’s embassy in South Africa did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

South Africa is battling wildlife smuggling on several fronts, from poached rhino horns and the bones of illegally farmed tigers to abalone shellfish and succulent plants.

The environment ministry said: “The illegal collection and trafficking of parrot eggs pose a serious threat to wild bird populations and animal welfare. Eggs are often concealed in improvised incubation devices and transported under conditions that significantly compromise their viability and endanger the welfare of developing embryos and hatchlings.”

Staff at the National Zoological Garden in Pretoria are incubating the seized eggs, the ministry said. “Several of the rescued eggs have successfully hatched and the chicks are receiving intensive veterinary and husbandry care to maximise their chances of survival,” the statement added.

The ministry said the arrests were carried out after a “joint intelligence-driven operation” led by its Environmental Management Inspectorate, known as the “Green Scorpions”, and police intelligence, border and endangered species units.

South Africa punishes the illegal export of Cites-listed species with a fine of 10m rand (£460,000), up to 10 years in prison or both.
